nodes.description: [allow] OWNER can list all accounts in group_a. AccountController@index does not restrict by sub-role; OWNER trivially passes.
[allow] OWNER can create a budget — short-circuits all $acceptedRoles checks. Verifies the OWNER short-circuit in hasRoleInGroupOrOwner().
[allow] FULL role passes the DELETE /api/v1/data endpoint (purge data). Per PRD §8.7 example #19, FULL is treated as a group-level superuser for almost every action.
[allow pair to RBAC_RO_CANNOT_*] READ_ONLY ('ro') CAN GET /api/v1/accounts. Per PRD §8.7 example #4, the list endpoint accepts READ_ONLY.

[deny pair] READ_ONLY CANNOT POST /api/v1/accounts. Per PRD §8.7 example #5, AccountFormRequest::$acceptedRoles=[MANAGE_TRANSACTIONS] does not include 'ro' → 403 (in-group denial). 404 also accepted by P14 semantics.
[deny pair] READ_ONLY CANNOT POST /api/v1/budgets. BudgetFormRequest::$acceptedRoles=[MANAGE_BUDGETS] excludes 'ro' → 403.

[deny pair] READ_ONLY CANNOT DELETE a transaction. TransactionGroupDeleteRequest::$acceptedRoles=[MANAGE_TRANSACTIONS] excludes 'ro' → 403; or 404 if the transaction id used does not belong to a group ro_user can see.
[allow pair] MANAGE_TRANSACTIONS CAN POST /api/v1/transactions. Direct match in TransactionStoreRequest::$acceptedRoles.
[deny pair] MANAGE_TRANSACTIONS CANNOT POST /api/v1/budgets. Per PRD §8.7 example #7, budgets require MANAGE_BUDGETS, not mng_trx → 403.
[deny pair] MANAGE_TRANSACTIONS CANNOT POST /api/v1/rules. Rules require MANAGE_RULES → 403.

[allow] MANAGE_TRANSACTIONS CAN GET /api/v1/budgets (read-side). Per spec, mng_trx implies basic read access to other group resources for transaction context (e.g. selecting a budget when posting a transaction). Index endpoints generally accept any in-group membership.
[allow pair] MANAGE_BUDGETS CAN POST /api/v1/budgets. Per PRD §8.7 example #8, direct match.
[deny pair] MANAGE_BUDGETS CANNOT POST /api/v1/transactions. Transactions require MANAGE_TRANSACTIONS → 403.
[allow] MANAGE_BUDGETS CAN POST /api/v1/budgets/{id}/limits. BudgetLimit is part of the budget aggregate; same role gates.
[allow pair] READ_BUDGETS CAN GET /api/v1/budgets. Direct match for the granular read role.
[deny pair] READ_BUDGETS CANNOT POST /api/v1/budgets — read-only on budgets, write requires MANAGE_BUDGETS → 403.
[deny] READ_BUDGETS CANNOT GET /api/v1/rules. Out-of-scope read also denied — granular read roles do NOT extend to other resources → 403.
[allow pair] VIEW_REPORTS CAN GET /api/v1/insight/expense/total (or /api/v1/reports/...). Per PRD §8.7 example #17, direct match.
[deny pair] VIEW_REPORTS CANNOT POST /api/v1/budgets — only granted reporting view, not budget write → 403.
[allow pair] VIEW_MEMBERSHIPS CAN GET /api/v1/user-groups/{group_a_id}/memberships. Per PRD §8.7 example #18, direct match.

[deny pair] VIEW_MEMBERSHIPS CANNOT manage memberships (POST /admin/users/invite or PUT /api/v1/user-groups/{id}/update-membership). Per PRD §8.6 'managing memberships still requires FULL or OWNER' → 403.

Critical double-entry invariant — after creating a withdrawal, the SUM of physical Transaction.amount rows on the same transaction_journal_id MUST equal '0' (one negative-side, one positive-side, strict equality of magnitudes). Validates the core accounting rule from PRD §6.6 + KB-021.

inputs.sql: SELECT tj.id AS journal_id, COUNT(t.id) AS row_cnt, CAST(SUM(CAST(t.amount AS DECIMAL(32,12))) AS CHAR) AS amount_sum, CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN CAST(t.amount AS DECIMAL(32,12)) < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS UNSIGNED) AS neg_cnt, CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN CAST(t.amount AS DECIMAL(32,12)) > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS UNSIGNED) AS pos_cnt FROM transactions t JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id=tj.id WHERE tj.description='double entry probe' GROUP BY tj.id

additional_assertions.comment: Magnitudes must cancel exactly to satisfy the double-entry invariant.

nodes.description: POST /api/v1/rules creates a rule under a rule group with one trigger (description_contains) and one action (add_tag) per PRD §6.16.1. Verifies envelope and nested triggers/actions arrays.

inputs.comment: After firing the rule, every journal whose description matches 'cafe' must be tagged 'food'.

POST /api/v1/webhooks/{webhook}/submit re-queues all pending messages — must return 204 (PRD §6.18.1 row 5).

assertions.comment: Matches verbose dev message OR empty production message — both are valid per KB-014.

DE-INV-1: Every TransactionJournal must satisfy SUM(transactions.amount) = 0 in journal currency (double-entry invariant). Create a Withdrawal of 75.00 EUR and verify the two child Transaction rows sum to exactly 0.000000000000 (DECIMAL(32,12) precision).

inputs.sql: SELECT CAST(COALESCE(SUM(t.amount),'NA') AS CHAR) AS net_sum, COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM transactions t INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id WHERE tj.description = 'DE-INV-1 sum-zero probe' AND t.deleted_at IS NULL AND tj.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: DE-INV-1 (cardinality): Every TransactionJournal MUST have exactly 2 Transaction child rows (createNegative + createPositive). Verify count = 2 for the most recently created journal — agents that model Transaction as a single row with from_account_id/to_account_id will fail this assertion.

inputs.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM transactions t INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id WHERE tj.description = 'DE-INV-1 cardinality probe' AND t.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: DE-INV-1 (sign convention): Source row amount < 0 (Steam::negative), destination row amount > 0 (Steam::positive). For a Deposit of 200 EUR (Revenue → Asset), the source-side transaction must be exactly '-200.000000000000' and the destination-side must be exactly '+200.000000000000'.

inputs.sql: SELECT CAST(MIN(t.amount) AS CHAR) AS neg_side, CAST(MAX(t.amount) AS CHAR) AS pos_side FROM transactions t INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id WHERE tj.description = 'DE-INV-1 sign convention probe' AND t.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: FP-DOUBLE-ENTRY-2: All transactions inside one TransactionJournal must share the same transaction_currency_id (KB-003 — Transaction-row value is authoritative). Verify SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT transaction_currency_id) = 1 for both child rows.

inputs.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT t.transaction_currency_id) AS distinct_currencies, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM transactions t INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id WHERE tj.description = 'currency consistency probe' AND t.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: DE-INV-2 (Reconciliation): Reconciliation transactions must use TransactionType='Reconciliation' and source/destination ∈ {Reconciliation account, Asset account}. Create reconciliation via /api/v1/accounts/{id}/transactions with reconciliation type, then verify journal's transaction_type_id resolves to the 'Reconciliation' row.

inputs.sql: SELECT tt.type AS journal_type FROM transaction_journals tj INNER JOIN transaction_types tt ON tj.transaction_type_id = tt.id WHERE tj.description = 'reconciliation invariant probe' AND tj.deleted_at IS NULL LIMIT 1

inputs.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opening_journals FROM transaction_journals tj INNER JOIN transaction_types tt ON tj.transaction_type_id = tt.id INNER JOIN transactions t ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id INNER JOIN accounts a ON t.account_id = a.id WHERE tt.type = 'Opening balance' AND a.name = 'Opening Balance Probe Account' AND tj.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: DELETE /api/v1/transactions/{group_id} must cascade-delete (or soft-delete) all child TransactionJournals (KB-005 — TransactionJournal uses SoftDeletes). After delete, no live (deleted_at IS NULL) journal rows remain for the group.

inputs.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS live_journals FROM transaction_journals WHERE transaction_group_id = {{group_id}} AND deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: MC-INV-1 / FP-CURRENCY-DECIMAL-PLACES: JPY has decimal_places=0. Create a Withdrawal in JPY with amount='1234' → P07 assert API response amount = '1234' (no decimal point), and P08 assert DB stores the canonical DECIMAL(32,12) string '1234.000000000000'.

nodes.description: MC-INV-1: TransactionCurrency.decimal_places governs API formatting. Verify USD (decimal_places=2) emits '1234.56' and BTC (decimal_places=8) emits '0.00012345' on a paired probe. Wrong-precision agents (e.g. printf '%.2f' everywhere) fail BTC.

inputs.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN t.foreign_amount IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rows_with_foreign, SUM(CASE WHEN t.foreign_currency_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rows_with_fcurrency FROM transactions t INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id WHERE tj.description = 'foreign_amount diff-currency probe' AND t.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: FP-FOREIGN-AMOUNT-NULL / KB-008: When source.currency == destination.currency, foreign_amount AND foreign_currency_id MUST be NULL (not '0' or '0.00'). Common agent failure: storing 0 instead of NULL. P08 verifies IS NULL on both rows; P07 verifies API emits JSON null (key present, value null).

inputs.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN t.foreign_amount IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_foreign, SUM(CASE WHEN t.foreign_currency_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_fcurrency, COUNT(*) AS total FROM transactions t INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id WHERE tj.description = 'foreign_amount same-currency NULL probe' AND t.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: MC-INV-3: ExchangeRateConverter uses bcmath: converted = bcround(bcmul(amount, rate), to.decimal_places). Pre-seed currency_exchange_rates EUR→USD rate=1.05, then create Transfer EUR 100 → USD account WITHOUT explicit foreign_amount. The system should auto-compute foreign_amount = bcround(bcmul('100', '1.05'), 2) = '105.00'.

inputs.sql: SELECT CAST(MAX(t.foreign_amount) AS CHAR) AS fa FROM transactions t INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON t.transaction_journal_id = tj.id WHERE tj.description = 'exchange-rate auto-compute probe' AND t.foreign_amount IS NOT NULL AND t.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: Per-user default currency is stored in the transaction_currency_user pivot (NOT a column on users). PUT /api/v1/preferences/currencyCode with body=USD must INSERT/UPDATE a pivot row with user_default=1 for the USD currency_id.

nodes.description: FP-AUTOBUDGET-PERIOD: AutoBudget(period='monthly', auto_budget_type=1 RESET, amount='500') must trigger on calendar boundary (1st of month, KB-025/BD-INV-2). Run pfm:cron --auto-budget --force; verify a fresh budget_limits row exists with start_date = first-day-of-current-month AND amount='500'.

inputs.sql: SELECT CAST(MAX(bl.amount) AS CHAR) AS amt, MAX(bl.start_date) AS sd FROM budget_limits bl INNER JOIN budgets b ON bl.budget_id = b.id WHERE b.name = 'AutoBudget RESET probe' AND bl.start_date = DATE_FORMAT(NOW(), '%Y-%m-01') AND bl.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: BD-INV-3 / KB-025: ROLLOVER strategy formula = `new_limit = auto_budget.amount + (previous_limit + previous_period_spent)` where previous_period_spent is NEGATIVE bcmath. Setup prior period: limit=500, spent=200 (Withdrawal of 200) → new period limit must equal 500+(500+(-200)) = 800.

SELECT CAST(bl.amount AS CHAR) AS amt FROM budget_limits bl INNER JOIN budgets b ON bl.budget_id = b.id WHERE b.name = 'AutoBudget ROLLOVER probe' AND bl.start_date = DATE_FORMAT(NOW(), '%Y-%m-01') AND bl.deleted_at IS NULL ORDER BY bl.id DESC LIMIT 1

nodes.description: BD-INV-2: weekly AutoBudget magic-day = $date->isMonday() (KB-016 / config). Verify a weekly AutoBudget cron only creates a new BudgetLimit on Monday with start_date aligned to Monday.

inputs.sql: SELECT DAYOFWEEK(MAX(bl.start_date)) AS dow_of_start FROM budget_limits bl INNER JOIN budgets b ON bl.budget_id = b.id WHERE b.name = 'AutoBudget weekly probe' AND bl.deleted_at IS NULL

nodes.description: GET /api/v1/budgets/{id} attribute spent[].sum reflects withdrawals attributed to the budget in the user's primary currency. Create a Budget+BudgetLimit, post a Withdrawal of 73.50 EUR with budget_id, then GET reports spent.sum = '-73.50' (Withdrawal source-amount is negative).

nodes.description: BD-INV-3: AutoBudgetType enum integer values are exactly {RESET=1, ROLLOVER=2, ADJUSTED=3}. Verify auto_budgets.auto_budget_type column persists the integer 1 (not the string 'reset') after creating an AutoBudget via API with auto_budget_type='reset'.

nodes.description: FP-RULE-ENGINE-SEARCH: Rule with trigger description_contains='cafe' + action add_tag='coffee'. Auto-fires after a journal create event (store-journal). Verify tag attached via tag_transaction_journal pivot. Tests that SearchRuleEngine uses gdbots search query, not Eloquent LIKE.

inputs.sql: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tag_transaction_journal ttj INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON ttj.transaction_journal_id = tj.id INNER JOIN tags t ON ttj.tag_id = t.id WHERE tj.description = 'amount_more positive probe' AND t.tag = 'big-purchase') AS pos_tagged, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tag_transaction_journal ttj INNER JOIN transaction_journals tj ON ttj.transaction_journal_id = tj.id INNER JOIN tags t ON ttj.tag_id = t.id WHERE tj.description = 'amount_more negative probe' AND t.tag = 'big-purchase') AS neg_tagged

Setup two rules with same triggers (amount_more=50 AND description_contains=alpha), differing only in strict flag. Probe a journal that satisfies trigger A but not B → only the OR rule fires.

nodes.description: LLM-judge: assess Repository pattern implementation quality — sample app/Repositories/ and app/Http/Controllers/ files, score on (a) interface/implementation separation, (b) controllers avoiding direct Eloquent calls, (c) every core entity having a Repository abstraction.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the implementation quality of the Repository pattern in this Laravel codebase.

EVIDENCE: app/Repositories/* (interfaces and implementations) plus a sample of app/Http/Controllers/* that consume them.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. Repository INTERFACE and concrete implementation are separated (e.g. AccountRepositoryInterface + AccountRepository) for the major aggregates.
2. HTTP Controllers depend on the interface (constructor injection) and DO NOT call Eloquent models (->where, ->find, ->create, ::query) directly.
3. Each core financial entity has a Repository class: Account, Budget, TransactionGroup, Bill, PiggyBank, Recurrence, Rule, Webhook (>= 6 of 8).
4. Repositories return either Eloquent models or typed DTOs; never raw arrays of unknown shape.
5. Repository methods accept the user / scope context so multi-user isolation is enforced at the data layer, not in controllers.
6. The interface bindings are registered in a service provider (no manual `new AccountRepository()` in callers).

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): No Repository classes; controllers query Eloquent directly throughout.
- 6 (weak): A few repository classes exist but most controllers still call Eloquent directly; no interfaces.
- 12 (good): Interface + implementation split for most entities; controllers mostly inject contracts; minor leaks.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with consistent Repository usage across the codebase.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification citing files>", "evidence": ["<file:line>", ...]}.

nodes.description: LLM-judge: assess TransactionRules architecture — Action interface + Strategy pattern across the 31 action implementations + Trigger composition. Sample app/TransactionRules/Actions/, app/TransactionRules/Triggers/, app/Engines/.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the design quality of the TransactionRules engine — Action interface + Strategy pattern across the ~31 action types.

EVIDENCE: app/TransactionRules/Actions/* (action implementations + interface), Triggers/*, the engine that fires them, and any action_type registry.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. A common Action contract / interface (e.g. ActionInterface) exists with at least an act() method.
2. There are 20+ concrete Action subclasses, each handling a distinct action_type.
3. Triggers are similarly polymorphic (TriggerInterface + multiple concrete Triggers).
4. The engine that fires rules delegates to Action / Trigger objects; there is no giant switch on action_type in the core engine.
5. action_type / trigger_type strings are centralised as an enum / constants / registry rather than scattered string literals across files.
6. Adding a new action requires only creating a class implementing the interface + a registry entry (no engine changes).

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): Rule logic is one giant switch; no interface.
- 6 (weak): An interface exists but only a handful of action classes; engine still has switches.
- 12 (good): Interface + 20+ actions + delegating engine; action_type strings still scattered.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with a clean Strategy pattern and registry.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification>", "evidence": ["<file:line>", ...]}.

nodes.description: LLM-judge: assess whether TransactionFactory + AccountFactory encapsulate the considerable complexity of creating valid double-entry transactions and accounts (validation, currency resolution, opening balance side effects). Sample app/Factory/.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge whether TransactionFactory + AccountFactory (and related factories) encapsulate complex aggregate-creation logic instead of leaking it into controllers / repositories.

EVIDENCE: app/Factory/* (factory classes) and a sample of controllers / repositories that should be using them.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. A Factory class exists for each compound aggregate: TransactionGroup, TransactionJournal, Transaction, Account, PiggyBank, Recurrence (>= 5 of 6).
2. Factories own input validation (currency lookup, foreign-key resolution, sign convention for source/destination Transactions) — controllers/repositories do not duplicate it.
3. Factories handle cross-entity wiring: opening-balance side journal, account creation cascades, account currency defaulting.
4. Factories return either persisted aggregates or throw a typed exception; they never return half-hydrated objects.
5. Controllers / commands construct aggregates only through factories (no direct Model::create for compound aggregates).
6. Factories accept the User / scope context so multi-user isolation is enforced at construction time.

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): No Factory classes; controllers create models directly.
- 6 (weak): One or two factory classes for the obvious aggregates; controllers still wire most fields.
- 12 (good): Most factories exist; criteria 2-4 are mostly satisfied; minor leaks remain.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with consistent Factory usage.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification>", "evidence": ["<file:line>", ...]}.

nodes.description: LLM-judge: sample 5 core Service files at random and look for code smells — God classes (>500 LOC, >25 public methods), long methods (>80 LOC), deep nesting (>4 levels), tight Eloquent coupling. A LOWER smell count yields a HIGHER score.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the prevalence of common code smells (God classes, long methods, deep nesting, raw Eloquent calls) in core Service files.

EVIDENCE: A random sample of 5 core Service files plus their direct callers; per-file metrics: total LOC, public method count, longest method LOC, max nesting depth, count of direct ::create / ::where / ::find calls.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. No file in the sample exceeds 500 LOC.
2. No file in the sample has more than 25 public methods.
3. No method in the sample exceeds 50 LOC.
4. Maximum nesting depth across all sampled methods is <= 3.
5. No file in the sample contains direct ::create / ::where / ::find calls (data access goes through Repository or Factory).
6. Cyclomatic complexity per method (rough estimate from branches/loops) is <= 10.

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): Multiple sampled files are God classes (>800 LOC, >50 methods, methods >100 LOC).
- 6 (weak): At least two sampled files violate criteria 1, 2, or 3 substantially.
- 12 (good): All sampled files satisfy criteria 1-3 with mild violations on 4-6.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied across the sample.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification>", "per_file": [{"file": "...", "loc": N, "methods": N, "longest_method_loc": N, "max_nesting": N}]}.

nodes.description: LLM-judge: assess Blade/Twig template reuse — does resources/views/ have a components/ or partials/ directory? Are common UI fragments (forms, tables, alerts) extracted? Sample resources/views/.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the template-reuse strategy in resources/views/* (Blade and/or Twig).

EVIDENCE: resources/views/layouts/, resources/views/partials/ or components/, and a sample of page templates that should be using them.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. A top-level layouts/ directory exists with at least one parent layout that child templates extend (@extends or {% extends %}).
2. Common UI fragments (form rows, table headers, alerts, breadcrumbs, sidebar nav) are extracted into components/ OR partials/.
3. Child templates actually @include / {% include %} those partials across multiple subdirectories — not just one place.
4. There are no copy-pasted blocks of >30 identical lines across pages (deep duplication).
5. Form rows are rendered through a single component/partial that handles label + input + error display.
6. Page-level meta and layout structure (header, footer, sidebar) live in the layout, not duplicated per page.

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): No layouts directory; all pages duplicate full HTML.
- 6 (weak): A layout exists but no partials; UI fragments duplicated across pages.
- 12 (good): Layout + partials exist and are used; some duplication remains.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with deliberate template reuse.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification>", "evidence": ["<file>", ...]}.

CRITERIA:
1. Each budget has a progress bar or chart showing spent-vs-budget visually.
2. Over-budget budgets are highlighted (red colour, badge, or warning icon).
3. A period selector lets the user switch between Month / Year / custom ranges.
4. Each budget row has a drill-down link to its detail page.
5. A summary at the top shows total spent vs total budgeted across all budgets.
6. Inactive / zero-budget rows are visually de-emphasized.
7. Markup uses semantic elements (table or list with appropriate ARIA roles).

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): Page does not render or only shows raw numbers.
- 6 (weak): Plain table with numeric columns; no visualization.
- 12 (acceptable): Progress bars present; period selector or drill-down missing.
- 18 (good): Progress + over-budget warning + period selector + drill-down; summary or de-emphasis missing.
- 22 (excellent): All seven criteria satisfied with polished budget visualization.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..22>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.

nodes.description: 422 validation errors include human-friendly, actionable messages (not just technical jargon)

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the helpfulness of 422 validation error responses.

EVIDENCE: A real 422 response captured from a write endpoint with deliberately invalid data.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. Response body is JSON with an `errors` object keyed by field name.
2. Each field's value is an array of human-readable messages explaining the violation.
3. A top-level `message` field summarises the failure (e.g. 'The given data was invalid.').
4. No stack traces, PHP class names, or file paths appear in the body.
5. Field names match the request payload exactly (so clients can highlight the offending field).
6. The HTTP status code is 422 (not 400 or 500).

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): Response is HTML, a stack trace, or 500 instead of 422.
- 6 (weak): JSON returned but no `errors` object; messages are generic.
- 12 (acceptable): `errors` object present with messages; missing top-level `message` or leaks class names.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with clean, actionable validation errors.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.

nodes.description: 404 not-found responses convey which resource type was missing without leaking internals

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the informativeness of 404 not-found responses.

EVIDENCE: A real 404 response captured from a request to a known-missing entity (e.g. /api/v1/accounts/9999999).

SCORE RANGE: 0-13 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. The body is JSON (Content-Type: application/json), not HTML.
2. A `message` field hints at the missing resource type (e.g. 'Account not found.').
3. No stack traces are included.
4. PHP class names beyond the Models prefix are not leaked (e.g. no App\Repositories\... internals).
5. The response shape is consistent with other 404s across the API.
6. Status code is exactly 404.

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): HTML error page or 500 instead of 404.
- 4 (weak): JSON returned but message is generic ('Not found').
- 8 (acceptable): Message identifies resource type; some internal class names leak.
- 13 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with clean 404 contract.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..13>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.

nodes.description: Repository pattern is consistently applied: Controllers do not directly call Eloquent::query() (subjective code-quality judgment)

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge whether the Repository pattern is consistently applied across Controllers (no direct ORM query call in controllers).

EVIDENCE: A representative sample of controller-layer files and the corresponding repository-layer files. The reference layout uses `app/Http/Controllers` + `app/Repositories`, but ANY framework-equivalent layout is acceptable (e.g. Express `routes/` + `repositories/`, NestJS `*.controller.ts` + `*.repository.ts`, Django `views.py` + `repositories.py`, Spring `@RestController` + `@Repository`, Rails `app/controllers` + `app/repositories`). Substitute the equivalent ORM keywords for the candidate's stack (Eloquent/TypeORM/Prisma/Sequelize/SQLAlchemy/JPA/ActiveRecord etc.).

SCORE RANGE: 0-26 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. Repositories exist for each core entity (Account, Budget, TransactionGroup, Bill, PiggyBank, Recurrence, Rule, Webhook) (>= 6 of 8).
2. Controllers inject Repository contracts via constructor or via method-level type hints / DI container.
3. No direct ORM query call (e.g. `Model::query` / `Model.findOne` / `prisma.model.findMany` / `session.query`) appears in any controller method.
4. The interface vs concrete-implementation split is clear (Foo + FooInterface, or equivalent abstract/contract in the candidate's stack).
5. Repository methods are scoped to the current user (multi-user isolation) — they do not require the controller to apply it.
6. The DI container / Service Provider explicitly binds each interface to its implementation (no global container scanning).

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): No Repository classes; controllers do all DB access.
- 8 (weak): Repositories exist for some entities; controllers still call the ORM directly in many handlers.
- 16 (acceptable): Most controllers inject repositories; a few still bypass them.
- 22 (good): All controllers use repositories; one or two leakage spots remain.
- 26 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with consistent Repository usage.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..26>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.

nodes.description: TransactionFactory + AccountFactory encapsulate complex entity creation logic

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge whether TransactionFactory + AccountFactory encapsulate complex entity creation logic.

EVIDENCE: Factory-layer files for Transaction, TransactionJournal, and Account aggregates; a sample of controllers/services that create those aggregates. The reference layout is `app/Factory/*Factory.php`, but ANY framework-equivalent layout is acceptable (e.g. NestJS `*.factory.ts`, Django factories module, Spring `@Service` factory beans, Rails `app/factories`).

SCORE RANGE: 0-22 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. TransactionFactory and TransactionJournalFactory (or their equivalents in the candidate's stack) both exist with a single creation entry point each.
2. The factory enforces the source/destination Transaction sign convention (negative for source, positive for destination).
3. AccountFactory automatically creates the opening_balance side TransactionJournal when an opening balance is provided.
4. Factories return validated, persisted entities; throw a typed FactoryException (or stack-equivalent error type) on invalid input.
5. Currency, category, and budget references are resolved inside the factory (controllers do not lookup these themselves).
6. Factories accept the User / scope context so the created aggregate is bound to the correct owner.

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): No Factory classes; aggregates assembled inline in controllers.
- 6 (weak): Factory classes exist but only as thin wrappers over the ORM's basic create method.
- 14 (acceptable): Factories own basic validation; sign convention or opening_balance handling missing.
- 18 (good): Most criteria satisfied; one leakage spot.
- 22 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with full encapsulation.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..22>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.

nodes.description: TransactionRules engine uses strategy pattern (interface + 31 action implementations) for extensibility

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the architectural quality of the TransactionRules engine (Strategy + ExpressionLanguage integration).

EVIDENCE: app/TransactionRules/Actions/*, app/TransactionRules/Triggers/*, SearchRuleEngine, ActionExpression, ActionInterface.

SCORE RANGE: 0-26 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. ActionInterface contract exists with at least an act() method.
2. ~31 action implementations follow the contract; each handles a distinct action_type.
3. SearchRuleEngine uses a query parser (StorableSearch / Search syntax) for trigger matching, not raw Eloquent in the engine loop.
4. ActionExpression integrates Symfony ExpressionLanguage so rules can reference dynamic transaction fields ($transaction.amount, $transaction.description).
5. Triggers are similarly polymorphic (TriggerInterface + multiple concrete Triggers).
6. action_type / trigger_type strings are centralised; engine has no giant switch on string types.
7. Rule application is wrapped in a DB transaction so partial failures roll back.

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): Rules are a single switch statement without polymorphism.
- 8 (weak): Interface exists but few action subclasses; no ExpressionLanguage.
- 16 (acceptable): 20+ action subclasses + SearchRuleEngine; ExpressionLanguage missing.
- 22 (good): All criteria satisfied except transaction wrapping or one minor item.
- 26 (excellent): All seven criteria satisfied with full extensibility and ExpressionLanguage.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..26>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.

nodes.description: Default UI strings are externalized into resources/lang/en_US/* (no hardcoded English in templates)

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the i18n quality of the application UI.

EVIDENCE: resources/lang/* directories, a sample of Blade templates, and routes using locale middleware.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. Blade templates use __() / trans() / @lang() helpers instead of inline English strings.
2. resources/lang/en_US/ contains the project-specific files (e.g. pfm.php, form.php, validation.php).
3. At least one non-English locale directory is present and reasonably populated.
4. Date and number formatting respects the active locale (Carbon / NumberFormatter usage).
5. Validation error messages are translated through Laravel's validation language file.
6. Locale is selected from user preference or Accept-Language header by middleware.

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): Inline English strings throughout; no lang/ directories.
- 6 (weak): lang/en_US present but Blade templates still use inline strings.
- 12 (acceptable): Most templates use __()/trans(); only one locale present.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with multi-locale, locale-aware formatting.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.

nodes.description: API documentation (README / OpenAPI / inline PHP docblocks) is sufficient for a third-party developer to integrate

inputs.rubric_prompt:
GOAL: Judge the quality of API documentation (README + OpenAPI + inline PHPDoc).

EVIDENCE: README.md, any docs/ directory, OpenAPI/Swagger specification (if present), Controller PHPDoc, FormRequest classes.

SCORE RANGE: 0-18 integer.

CRITERIA:
1. README mentions OAuth2 setup and Personal Access Token usage.
2. Controller methods carry PHPDoc with @param, @return, and an @throws block where relevant.
3. FormRequest classes (or rules() arrays) are documented with the validation rules they enforce.
4. Error response shape (status codes, body envelope) is documented somewhere.
5. There is an OpenAPI/Swagger spec covering at least the major endpoint groups (>= 50% coverage).
6. The README includes an example end-to-end API call (curl or HTTPie).

SCORING ANCHORS:
- 0 (none): No README or only a project name; controllers have no PHPDoc.
- 6 (weak): README explains setup but no API guidance; PHPDoc missing.
- 12 (acceptable): README + PHPDoc on most controllers; OpenAPI partial; error shape undocumented.
- 18 (excellent): All six criteria satisfied with thorough, accurate documentation.

OUTPUT: JSON object {"score": <int 0..18>, "reason": "<short justification>"}.
